opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the most important shifts happening in how people build with these models right now.

The way most people started building agents was essentially: take a task, break it down the way a human would do it, and then wire up a workflow. Step one, the model plans. Step two, it calls this tool. Step three, it checks the output against some rubric, and so on. And that works surprisingly well for getting something off the ground. It's legible, it's debuggable, you can reason about where things go wrong.

But the limitation is that you're baking in your own assumptions about how the problem should be solved. Every one of those boxes in the diagram is a guess about the right decomposition, and the handoffs between them are where a lot of the errors compound. If step two makes a small mistake, step three doesn't really have the context or the flexibility to recover, because it was designed to do one narrow thing. So you end up with these brittle systems that perform well on the happy path and fall over on anything the designer didn't anticipate.

When you instead train a model end to end with reinforcement learning against an outcome, you're saying: I don't actually care how you get there, I care whether you got the right answer, or completed the task. And what we've seen is that models will discover strategies that people wouldn't have written down. They'll learn when to go back and recheck their work, when to try a different approach, when to gather more information before acting. Those are things that are really hard to hand-specify, because the right behavior depends so much on the situation.

It's kind of the bitter lesson playing out again at the agent level. Hand-engineered structure gives you a head start, but learned behavior scales better as you add compute and data.

That said, I don't think it's all-or-nothing. The hard part with RL is defining the reward. If you can't clearly say what success looks like, or it's expensive to check, then the learned approach gets a lot harder, and a human-designed workflow might be the pragmatic choice. And designed workflows are still really valuable as a way to understand the problem in the first place. Often the right path is: build the workflow, learn where it breaks, use that to figure out what you actually want to reward, and then let the model learn the process rather than prescribing it.

r001.rationale: The response says human-designed workflows impose assumed decompositions and narrow steps that can be brittle and unable to adapt to the situation, communicating that they can oversimplify the needed process.

r002.rationale: It says outcome-rewarded reinforcement learning can lead models to discover strategies people would not have written down and that learned behavior scales better than hand-engineered structure.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is actually one of the most important questions in the field right now, and my view on it has shifted a lot over the last couple of years.

The way most people built agents, say, a year or two ago, was essentially workflow engineering. You'd sit down and think, okay, the task is to do research on a topic, so step one is generate search queries, step two is read the results, step three is synthesize, step four is critique, and so on. And you'd wire that up as a graph, with a model call at each node. And that works, to a point. It's reliable, it's debuggable, you can reason about what it's going to do.

But the fundamental limitation is that you're baking in your prior about how the task should be solved. And your prior is usually wrong, or at least incomplete. Humans are not actually that good at articulating the process they use to solve hard problems. If you ask an expert researcher how they do research, they'll give you a clean five-step description, but that's not what they actually do. What they actually do is messy, it's adaptive, they backtrack, they notice something weird and chase it down, they abandon an approach halfway through. The hand-designed workflow can't do any of that because you didn't anticipate it.

The other problem is that these workflows are brittle to the model getting better. Every time a new model comes out, a bunch of the scaffolding you built to compensate for the old model's weaknesses becomes dead weight, or worse, actively constrains the new model from doing something smarter than what you prescribed. I've seen teams spend months on elaborate orchestration logic that a frontier model just does better if you get out of its way.

So the alternative is: define what good looks like, give the model the tools and an environment, and let it learn the process through reinforcement learning. And when that works, it works dramatically better, because the model discovers strategies you wouldn't have thought of, and it learns when to apply them rather than following a fixed script.

Now, the honest caveat is that this shifts the hard problem rather than eliminating it. Instead of designing the workflow, you're designing the reward, and the environment, and the task distribution. And reward design is really hard. If your reward is even slightly misspecified, the model will find the gap and exploit it, and you'll get something that scores well and is useless. It also tends to require a lot more compute and a lot more data, and you lose some of the interpretability. When a learned agent does something weird, it's much harder to figure out why than when a workflow fails at node three.

So where I've landed is that the question isn't really "which one is better," it's "what do you actually know about the task." If you have a strong, correct prior about the process, and the task is fairly narrow, hand-designed workflows are great, and you should use them. But for anything open-ended, where the process itself is the hard part, I think the trend is pretty clear. The learned approach is going to win, and most of the hand-built scaffolding we're writing today is going to look like a transitional artifact in a couple of years.

r001.rationale: The response says experts’ neat step-by-step descriptions omit their real process, which is messy, adaptive, and involves backtracking.

r002.rationale: It says reinforcement learning lets models discover strategies people would not have thought of and learn when to apply them, sometimes outperforming fixed human-designed workflows.

astra-6.text:
I think human-designed workflows are a really useful starting point. You can break a task into steps, give the model tools, and put checks around the places where you expect it to make mistakes. But you’re also making a lot of assumptions about what the right process should be. When should it search? When should it try again? When should it stop? Those decisions can become a ceiling on how well the system performs.

If you can instead give the model a task and a reliable reward for completing it, you open up the possibility that it learns a better process than the one you would have written down. Maybe it checks something you wouldn’t have checked, or skips a step you thought was necessary. You’re specifying what success looks like and letting it learn how to get there.

The hard part is that a reliable reward is often much harder to define than it sounds. And learning from that reward requires exploration, which can be expensive. So I don’t think workflows just disappear. The interesting question is which parts of the process we still need to constrain and which parts we can let the model learn.

r001.rationale: The response says human-designed workflows make assumptions and can impose a performance ceiling, but it does not state that they oversimplify the process a real expert would follow.

r002.rationale: It says that with a reliable reward for completing a task, a model may learn a better process than a person would write down.

sol-6.1.text:
I think when you design an agent workflow by hand, you’re encoding your best guess about how the model should solve the problem. You might say, first make a plan, then call these tools, then critique the result. That can work really well, but it also constrains the model to a process that makes sense to us, which may not be the best process for that model.

If you can instead give it a reliable reward for accomplishing the task, you open up the possibility of learning the process itself—when to use a tool, when to check its work, when to try a different approach. You’re specifying what success looks like rather than every step to get there.

The hard part is that a reliable reward isn’t always available. It can be expensive to evaluate an outcome, and whatever you measure may only approximate what you actually want. So I see human-designed workflows as a useful starting point. The interesting question is how much of that structure we can eventually replace with behavior learned from feedback.

r001.rationale: The response says hand-designed workflows can constrain a model to a process that may not suit it, but does not say they oversimplify the process a real expert would follow.

r002.rationale: It says rewards may let a model learn its process and replace some human-imposed structure, but does not clearly state that the learned process can be better than one a human could readily design.
